nameStory: The mossy maze polypore gets its whimsical name from its unique undersurface that resembles a tiny labyrinth. Instead of the typical round pores you'd expect from most polypores, this fungus creates an intricate pattern of elongated, maze-like openings that twist and turn like passages in a miniature puzzle. The "mossy" part comes from its often grayish-green appearance that can blend beautifully with the moss-covered logs where it grows.
description: The mossy maze polypore is a bracket fungus that grows like a shelf or fan from dead hardwood trees and logs. It forms tough, leathery brackets that can be several inches across with a grayish to brownish upper surface that often develops zones of different colors. What makes this fungus special is its underside, which features distinctive maze-like pores instead of the round holes typical of most polypores. As a saprobic fungus, it helps decompose dead wood by causing white rot, breaking down the lignin and leaving behind whitish, fibrous wood.

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: The underside shows distinctive elongated, maze-like or slot-shaped pores that twist and interconnect, rather than round holes. These maze patterns are cream to pale yellow when fresh and feel slightly rough to the touch.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Tough, leathery brackets that are grayish-brown to darker brown on top, often with concentric zones of different shades. The surface feels dry and slightly velvety when young, becoming smoother with age.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Usually grows directly from wood without a stem, forming shelf-like brackets. Occasionally may have a very short, stubby attachment point.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels quite firm and leathery, not easily bent or broken. The brackets are persistent, staying on trees for months or even over a year.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Generally odorless or with a very faint, pleasant mushroomy smell. No strong or unpleasant odors.

habitat: Look for mossy maze polypore on dead hardwood trees and fallen logs throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests. It particularly favors oak, maple, beech, and birch, growing as overlapping brackets on stumps, dead standing trees, and well-decayed logs. You'll often find it in moist woodland areas where dead wood stays damp, from sea level up into the mountains.

seasonality.spring: Existing brackets from previous seasons are still visible and identifiable. New growth may begin on well-positioned dead wood as temperatures warm and spring rains provide moisture.
seasonality.summer: Active growing season with fresh, pale brackets appearing. This is when the maze-like pores are most clearly defined and the colors are at their most vibrant.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for finding fresh specimens as fall rains stimulate new growth. Brackets formed this season will be at their most diagnostic, with crisp pore patterns and distinct coloration.
seasonality.winter: Older brackets persist and remain identifiable throughout winter, though they may become darker and more weathered. The leathery texture helps them survive freezing temperatures.

funFact: The maze-like pore pattern of this fungus is so unique that it can actually change shape as the bracket grows, with round pores near the edge gradually elongating and connecting to form the characteristic labyrinth pattern toward the center - it's like watching a puzzle solve itself in slow motion!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with turkey tail, but turkey tail has a much thinner, more flexible texture and tiny round pores instead of maze-like ones. Remember: if you can easily bend it like paper, it's probably turkey tail; if it feels like leather and has maze pores, you've got mossy maze polypore.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "polypore" (meaning "many pores"), this fungus doesn't actually have typical round pores for most of its surface. This naming quirk reflects how fungal classification sometimes relies more on microscopic features and evolutionary relationships than on what we can easily see with our eyes.
compareHints: Since this is the only Cerrena species in our region, compare it with other maze-pored fungi in the greater polypore family. Daedalea quercina (oak mazegill) has similar maze-like pores but grows almost exclusively on oak and has a whiter, corky texture. Trametes species may have slightly elongated pores but never develop the true maze pattern of Cerrena unicolor.
